newsitem.title: USA: Senate sources hope to show links to foreign funds.
newsitem.headline: Senate sources hope to show links to foreign funds.

text.p: New information of links between Democratic fund-raiser John Huang and the Indonesian Lippo Group is expected to be presented by witnesses at a Tuesday Senate hearing, sources said on Monday.

Witnesses at the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on fund-raising abuses in the 1996 election will include former executives of Lippo Group and former employees of the Commerce Department where Huang worked from 1984-1996.

The sources, who asked not to be identified, said the evidence would include a letter allegedly tying Huang to contributions to Democrats by the Riadys, the wealthy Indonesian family that held control of Lippo, a real estate and financial business.
Foreign contributions to U.S. political campaigns are illegal if made by foreign nationals who are not legal U.S. residents or by foreign companies from profits made outside the United States.

The committee was briefed on Monday by government intelligence officials. Chairman Fred Thompson, Republican of Tennessee, last week made the accusation that high-level Chinese government officials crafted a plan to increase China's influence over the U.S. political process.
Thompson said his view was based on secret documents, many provided by the Justice Department.

The hearings last week focused on the role of Huang, a former Commerce Department official and former employee of Lippo who arranged some of the Democratic National Committee's most controversial fund-raising events during the 1996 campaign, including a dinner and a coffee meeting that brought Clinton into contact with foreign citizens.

He has so far refused to testify but has said he might do so if the committee were to give him "limited immunity" that would essentially protect him from any criminal charges except those concerning espionage or the passing of secrets.

Separately, the chairman of the House of Representatives committee investigating alleged campaign finance abuses asked on Monday for President Bill Clinton's help in obtaining evidence from a big Democratic contributor thought to have fled to Thailand.

House Government Reform Committee Chairman Dan Burton, an Indiana Republican, wrote Clinton and Thailand's ambassador to the United States Nitya Pibulsonggram to help obtain testimoney from Pauline Kanchanalak.
Burton said Kanchanalak may have "crucial knowledge" regarding fund-raising activities and the influence of foreign governments on U.S. politics.
Kanchanalak was believed to be in her native Thailand. She donated $235,000 to the Democratic National Committee which was returned by the party because its origin could not be verified.
